doc.title: Clyde Kerr Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 22, 2006

title: Mother's singing voice heard in his trumpet tone
summary: His mother sang in church; a 1974-75 tape showed him his trumpet tone resembles her alto voice, linked to his love of flugelhorn sound.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: I draw from because that’s a part of my experiences you know. My mother sang. She wasn’t a professional singer but she sang in church, that’s how my parents met, she sang in church, he heard her sing and that was like the beginning of me. But my mother had a beautiful, lyrical sound. And it’s a funny thing about it, some years later I found out my tone, my sound on my trumpet, sort of has the same quality of her voice. And thinking about that over the years, probably when I was still in her womb that she was singing, I heard that voice. And I remember as a kid when my mother used to speak on the phone I was sitting next to her on the side of the bed and put my ear to her back to hear the vibration. And it all just came together many years after that, that it probably was bringing me back to those days before I was out in the world to hear the vibrations come. And I didn’t know what I was doing at the time. The way I came to realize this is in 1974, ’75, I played a gig and I taped the gig and the next day I ran it through my stereo system at home. I was home alone, my family was out of town or something, and the music was playing and my trumpet was playing I was off from the room where I was playing. You know sometimes when you get away from something you can see it better, you can hear it better. And I thought I heard my mother say something to me. So I went in the room, I said, “Mom,” I was wondering how she got in my house you know, because she lived a little distance, she was living at the time. And she wasn’t there. So I went back and then I heard it again. So I focused in on the tape and I ran the tape back and I started listening a little bit more. Sure enough, man, some of the tones on my trumpet has the quality of her voice. She had a voice like a rich alto voice. And she sang, she wasn’t a jazz singer like bop, bebop and all this stuff, but she could carry just a beautiful pure melody the same way Ella Fitzgerald would sing a song with the correct diction and the flow of the voice. So all up until that time I was thinking that I got everything I have musically from my father because he was a trumpet player as well. But that made me realize, I said wow man, as long as I play I could hear my mother’s voice.
That’s a terrific story. I wonder if it might be part of the reason you were attracted to the flugelhorn also? To grab that alto—

Right, oh yeah. In fact before I had a flugelhorn I used to try to get the flugelhorn sound on my trumpet, to get that big rich, full, dark sound. And until today, now when I’m playing if my tone is not right then anything I play I’m not going to be pleased with it. First of all I’ve got to get my sound right. And then anything I play after that I’ll be pleased with it. But if it doesn’t sound right I don’t care what I play it’s not happening you know.

Isn’t it amazing how you take a piece of brass and most trumpets are basically the same, you know you can have a little bit different mouthpiece but you listen to the difference in one trumpet player to the next, it’s just unbelievable.
